lines: Knowing exactly what a page looks like only gets an engine so far.
A disk is slow enough that fetching the same page over and over would drag every query down with it.
So something has to decide, moment to moment, which pages are worth holding onto in memory and which ones can wait.
Here's that cache's own replacement scheme, read directly off a live cluster rather than assumed.
A hand sweeps past every slot in a fixed circle, never stopping to rank anything by how recently it was touched.
Each slot carries its own small counter, raised every time that slot gets used, and the hand only takes a slot whose counter has already fallen to nothing.
Worth checking what happens if that same small table keeps getting touched again and again.
Measured directly, the counter does keep climbing with each touch, but only up to a small ceiling.
Past that ceiling it simply stops, no matter how many more times the table gets scanned.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A scan that reads a table far bigger than the whole cache touches an enormous number of slots, but only once each.
Does sweeping past every one of those slots the ordinary way end up clearing out most of the cache to make room?
answer: It doesn't, and the reason is a second, separate trick this scheme reaches for.

A slot that's only ever touched by a once-through scan like that is unlikely to matter again soon, so a small, separate loop of slots gets reused for the whole scan instead of sweeping through the entire cache.
Nothing outside that small loop ever gets disturbed.

lines: Here's that separate loop shown directly, not just argued for.
A table built and scanned for real, with vastly more content than the whole cache could ever hold at once.
Measured right after the scan finishes, only a small, bounded slice of it actually ended up resident. The rest of the cache was never touched.
A completely different kind of bookkeeping is worth checking the same way.
A page just changed for real carries a marker, read directly, saying it still needs to be written out.
Run a real save point and check that exact same marker again: it's already flipped back to clean.
Worth naming one real cost of running a cache like this at all.
The operating system underneath is already caching the same bytes on its own, so an engine's own cache usually ends up holding a duplicate copy of everything.
One setting on the operating system exists specifically to skip that duplication, at the cost of the engine doing all of that caching work itself.
There happens to be a second cluster available here too, a genuinely newer release of the same engine.
That newer release really does run a documented approach to reading many pages at once instead of one at a time.
Scanning it for real shows the counters it keeps rising under exactly that approach, which is real, counted activity, not just a claim in a document.
Pulling the whole topic back together.
A sweeping hand and a small counter per slot, read directly rather than assumed, with a measured ceiling on how high that counter climbs.
A once-through scan that reuses a small, separate loop instead of clearing out the whole cache, measured directly after it ran.
A dirty marker that a real save point actually flips clean. Duplicate caching, and the one setting that skips it. And a second, newer cluster's own newer reading approach, measured for real.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
One once-through scan over a huge table finishes right before a second, unrelated once-through scan starts over a different, equally huge table.
Does the second scan get slowed down because the first one already used up the whole cache scanning its own table?
answer: It doesn't, for exactly the reason this topic already measured directly.
Each once-through scan reuses its own small, separate loop rather than claiming space across the whole cache, so the first scan never touches the rest of the cache at all.
There's nothing there for the second scan to find missing.
